editorNote: A bold graphics machine reaches for a place beyond strict IBM imitation, while games, accessibility and packaged software show just how many directions the microcomputer market is taking.
morningLine: The Mindset PC gambles on color, speed and a distinctive visual identity.

lead.headline: Mindset PC Bets on Custom Color Graphics
lead.dek: An 80186, MS-DOS and purpose-built video hardware aim the new machine at artists, animators and game makers.
body: The newest challenge to the IBM-shaped personal-computer market arrives with a very different sales pitch: do more with the picture. InfoWorld placed the Mindset computer on its March 19 cover under the teasing line “Gambling on Great Graphics,” giving the ambitious machine one of the week’s most conspicuous introductions.

Inside is Intel’s 80186 processor and MS-DOS, but the headline attraction is custom graphics hardware rather than strict IBM compatibility. The system can display 320 by 200 pixels with 16 colors at once, a specification meant to make painting, animation and game work feel native instead of added as an afterthought.

Mindset Designer supplies the showcase. The paint program’s tools and colorful sample art turn the computer into a visual workstation, and contemporary documentation identifies programmer Kevin Furry and artist Whitney Caughlan among the people behind the package.

That specialty is also the wager. Buyers now have abundant software and familiar IBM-compatible choices, so a distinctive display must justify stepping away from the safest standard. Mindset is betting that a vivid screen and responsive graphics can create a market of their own.

stories.headline: Microcomputers Become Tools of Independence
body: The March 19 InfoWorld cover also points toward a quieter revolution: personal computers adapted for people with disabilities. Period rehabilitation research compared machines from Apple, Epson, IBM and others as aids for communication, environmental control and information access.

The work treats the micro not merely as office equipment but as a flexible interface. Alternate input devices and specialized software can turn a general-purpose home computer into a practical bridge to writing, learning and control of everyday surroundings.

stories.headline: Laserdiscs Point Toward an Arcade-Style Future at Home
body: Computer & Video Games is asking whether laserdiscs can bring the spectacle of the new arcade cabinets into the living room. Full-motion filmed imagery promises a visual leap far beyond sprites, even if cost, storage and interaction still make the route uncertain.

The same March issue previews Atari’s Major Havoc and Marvin’s Maze and reviews joysticks across micros and video systems. Together they show a games market testing new pictures and new controls while home computers and consoles increasingly share the same shelf.

stories.headline: Chequered Flag Takes the British Micro Pole
body: The RAM/C all-formats chart published March 17 puts Sinclair’s Chequered Flag at No. 1, ahead of Manic Miner and Fighter Pilot. Atic Atac and Scuba Dive complete a top five packed with fast, inexpensive microcomputer play.

The list captures the variety of the Spectrum-era shelf: motor racing, platform action, flight simulation, maze adventure and undersea exploration. Ultimate Play the Game also has Lunar Jetman and Jetpac farther down the chart, evidence of a vigorous specialist software trade.
